items.passage: Manila Bay's lighthouse station had two keepers' cottages joined by a single wall, and for eleven years I shared it with Wira. We knocked twice each evening to say the lamp was lit. When the bureau assigned Mateo to replace her, I resented him on principle, and for weeks I let his knocks go unanswered. Then one night the generator failed, and Mateo climbed the tower with me, holding the flashlight steady while I reset the breaker. Afterward he asked how Wira used to signal, and I found myself teaching him the double knock. Keeping that small ritual alive, I realized, honored her more than my silence ever had. Below us, the fishing boats rocked in a row, their lanterns swinging like loose buttons on a coat.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To recount how the narrator and Mateo worked together to repair a generator that failed one night
To explain how the bureau organized the routines that keepers followed for lighting the lamp
To show how the narrator comes to see that welcoming a newcomer can preserve an old bond
To suggest that people must eventually let go of the past entirely in order to be happy
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 화자는 Wira와의 오랜 의리 때문에 새로 온 Mateo의 노크를 외면하지만, 뒷부분에서는 그에게 Wira의 두 번 노크를 가르치며 그 의식을 이어 가는 것이 오히려 Wira를 기리는 일임을 깨닫는다. 두 곳의 대비를 연결하면 새 이웃을 받아들이는 것이 옛 유대를 지키는 길이 될 수 있다는 C가 요지다. A는 발전기 수리 일화만 요약했고, B는 등대 소재를 쓰지만 서술 목적이 다르다. D는 과거를 완전히 버리라는 지나치게 일반적인 교훈으로, 지문은 오히려 과거를 이어 간다.

items.passage: “Leave the back panel; we only need to replace the shelf,” Okja said, handing over the chisel. In the quiet reading room of the Hokkaido library, Caoimhe pried loose the warped board and found an envelope wedged behind it, addressed in faded ink to someone named only as the Thursday reader. That morning the librarian had mentioned an elderly man who came every Thursday and always ran his hand along this very shelf before sitting down. Caoimhe studied the envelope, then cut a shallow groove into the new board, just deep enough to hold it. Okja raised an eyebrow but said nothing about the extra hour it cost. Outside, snow slid from the roof in a long, soft rush.
items.question: Based on the text, why does Caoimhe most likely cut a groove into the new board?
options: She worries that Okja will scold her for disturbing the back panel he told her to leave alone.
She hopes the extra hour of careful work will impress Okja with her skill as a carpenter.
She wants the envelope to stay where the man who visits on Thursdays might still find it.
She believes the library has a rule requiring any lost papers to be stored inside shelves.
items.explanation: 봉투가 'Thursday reader'에게 쓰여 있다는 점과, 사서가 말한 매주 목요일 이 선반을 손으로 쓸어 보는 노인이 있다는 점을 연결하면 Caoimhe가 편지를 원래 자리에 남겨 두려 한다는 동기가 드러난다. 따라서 C가 정답이다. A는 Okja에 대한 걱정이라는 다른 감정에서 나온 동기이고, B는 '추가 한 시간'이라는 결과를 동기로 착각한 것이다. D는 지문에 없는 도서관 규칙이라는 외부 원인을 끌어왔다.

items.passage: We crossed the dry bed of the river below Bergen that last evening, Ingeborg, you with your trunk strap over one shoulder and I, old Jens, carrying the lantern your father once carried for me. You leapt from stone to stone as though the scholarship letter in your pocket had made you lighter, and I confess my chest swelled to watch it. Seven winters I had tutored you at my kitchen table, and here was the proof that it had not been folly. Only when you paused to ask whether the water would return by spring did I think of the empty chair you would leave behind. Still, I told you it would, and I praised your steady feet. On the far bank, a cart stood waiting, its horse stamping at the cold gravel.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
options: Deep grief over a parting that the speaker expects to be permanent
Mournful regret that is only occasionally softened by flashes of pride
Uneasy suspicion about the hidden terms attached to the scholarship
Proud affection that is touched, more faintly, by a sense of loss
items.explanation: 화자는 장학금 편지를 가진 Ingeborg를 보며 가슴이 벅찼다고 하고 일곱 겨울의 가르침이 헛되지 않았다고 말하며, 마지막에도 그녀의 발걸음을 칭찬해 자부심과 애정이 두드러진다. 그 사이에 남겨질 빈 의자를 떠올리는 상실감이 한 번 스치므로 D가 가장 적절하다. A는 덜 두드러진 정서만 말했고, B는 두 정서의 비중을 뒤집었다. C의 의심은 장학금 소재와 어울리지만 지문에 단서가 없다.

items.passage: Rusted shears in hand, Annika knelt beside the tomato bed she and her brother Cyrus kept behind the community hall in Porto Alegre. That morning, hunting for twine in the shop's counter drawer, she had found a stack of overdue notices he had hidden beneath the receipt book. Now Cyrus arrived with two cups of coffee and a story about how well the week's sales had gone. Annika let him finish, then mentioned lightly that she had already sold her bicycle and would put the money toward the electricity bill. He stared at her, set down the cups, and quietly began tying up the vines she had missed. Across the garden, an old woman was scattering crushed eggshells around her lettuce.
items.question: Based on the text, which choice best describes the relationship between Annika and Cyrus?
options: They are siblings who each try to shield the other from the strain of the shop's troubles.
Annika resents Cyrus for hiding the shop's overdue notices and means to confront him.
Cyrus depends on Annika to make every decision about the shop and its unpaid bills.
They are rivals competing over the shop to prove which of them deserves to run it.
items.explanation: Cyrus는 연체 고지서를 서랍에 숨기고 매출이 좋았다고 이야기하며 Annika를 걱정시키지 않으려 하고, Annika는 그를 추궁하지 않고 자전거를 팔아 전기료에 보태겠다고 가볍게 말한다. 두 행동을 이어 읽으면 서로를 감싸 주려는 남매 관계, 즉 A가 드러난다. B는 Annika의 감정만 일부 반영했으며 실제로 그녀는 대립하지 않는다. C는 의존의 방향을 한쪽으로 몰았고, D는 형제 경쟁이라는 일반적 통념에서 나온 선택지다.

items.passage: Tar and wet hemp, that was the smell of every crossing. I was fourteen the summer Budi began riding our barge up the estuary from the Cornish coast, always with a sealed parcel on his knees and never with a fare in his hand. Father had told me only that Budi had once pulled him from the water at Falmouth, and that I, Abena, was not to ask for money. Each morning I spliced the frayed end of our mooring line, and each evening it had worn through again against the iron ring. Budi watched me work the strands together and once offered to buy us new rope. I said the old one would hold, and he did not argue. By September the splice was thicker than the rope itself, a knot of patches I could have tied blindfolded. On his last crossing he set his parcel down, took the line from me, and wove one strand in himself before stepping ashore without a word.
items.question: In the text, the repeatedly mended mooring line most likely represents
options: the ferryman's pride in the river skills he has passed down to his daughter.
the unspoken obligation that keeps the narrator's family and Budi bound together.
the growing danger of carrying passengers across the estuary in a worn barge.
the narrator's private wish to escape her father's trade on the river someday.
items.explanation: Budi는 아버지의 목숨을 구한 일 때문에 운임을 내지 않고, 아무도 그 빚을 말하지 않는다. 매일 끊어지고 다시 이어지는 밧줄, 새 밧줄을 사 주겠다는 제안을 거절하는 장면, 마지막에 Budi가 직접 한 가닥을 엮어 넣는 장면이 이어지며 밧줄은 양쪽을 묶는 말없는 의무를 상징하게 되므로 B가 정답이다. A는 기술 전수, C는 위험, D는 떠나고 싶은 마음을 말하지만 지문에 그런 단서가 없다.

items.passage: What do you say to a man who returns your present before he has even opened it? For three years I clerked for Bartolo in the courthouse above the harbor, and when he retired to take English lessons at a small language school in Valparaiso, I bought him a leather notebook for his vocabulary lists. On Tuesday he set it on my desk in the empty classroom, still in its tissue paper, and said he could not accept gifts from someone whose career he might yet be asked to recommend. His voice was the same one he had used from the bench, courteous and final. I held the package and felt I had been handed a verdict wrapped in tissue paper. Later, Camila, the teacher, asked me to help stack the chairs, and I did it slowly, listening to the gulls.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a verdict wrapped in tissue paper” most nearly suggests that the narrator
options: believes Bartolo has secretly decided to report her conduct to the court.
thinks the notebook was wrapped too carelessly to be offered as a gift.
experiences the return as a firm judgment delivered with gentle politeness.
suspects Bartolo is pretending to be stern to conceal his real gratitude.
items.explanation: Bartolo는 선물을 뜯지도 않고 돌려주며 원칙적인 이유를 대고, 그의 목소리는 법정에서처럼 '정중하지만 단호했다'. 이 두 단서를 연결하면 '판결'은 되돌릴 수 없는 단호한 결정을, '얇은 포장지'는 그것이 부드럽고 예의 바르게 전달되었음을 뜻하므로 C가 정답이다. A는 판결이라는 단어를 법적 고발로 지나치게 문자적으로 읽었고, B는 포장지를 문자 그대로 받아들였다. D는 지문에 근거가 없는 숨은 감사를 가정한다.

items.passage: By the third week of the monsoon, Sunethra had stopped expecting her father's letters and started counting the hives instead. Seven boxes stood along the wall of the yard in Karachi; the eighth had gone silent in April, its colony lost to mites. Lanying, who had shared a shop with her father before he sailed, came by most evenings to drink tea and talk of nothing in particular. She never mentioned bees. Yet one damp morning Sunethra lifted the lid of the eighth box and found it thick with a new swarm, the frames already beaded with wax. When she asked, Lanying only shrugged and spoke about the price of sugar. Her kindness, Sunethra thought, moved through the yard like smoke through a hive, calming everything and leaving nothing behind. That afternoon the rain came again, drumming on the tin roof of the shed.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “like smoke through a hive” most nearly suggests that Lanying's help was
options: irritating to the bees and unsettling to the rest of the yard.
brief and fleeting, so that Sunethra soon forgot about it.
heavy and oppressive, making the yard hard to breathe in.
quietly soothing and difficult to trace back to its source.
items.explanation: Lanying은 벌 이야기를 한 번도 꺼내지 않았고, 새 벌 떼에 대해 묻자 어깨만 으쓱하고 설탕 값 이야기로 넘어간다. 양봉에서 연기는 벌을 진정시키지만 흔적을 남기지 않으므로, 두 단서를 연결하면 그녀의 도움이 조용히 위로가 되면서도 출처를 드러내지 않았다는 D가 정답이다. A는 연기를 벌을 자극하는 것으로, C는 숨 막히는 것으로 오해한 해석이다. B는 금방 잊혔다고 하지만 Sunethra는 그 친절을 곱씹고 있다.

items.passage:
What would Ivy want, Ronan wondered,
now that an ocean sat between them
and the date they had always kept came round again?
Above Port of Spain the tea rows climbed
like green stitches holding the slope together,
and he walked them at dawn, as the two of them once had,
pinching the youngest leaves the way she taught him.
Last year she had written that she kept no calendars now,
that each new street was busy erasing the old ones.
So he would send no card, no ribbon, nothing she must answer.
He dried one handful of leaves on the windowsill
and mailed them folded in plain brown paper,
a small country she could steep and drink alone.
The pickers' songs drifted up from the lower terraces,
thin and bright in the cooling air.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a small country she could steep and drink alone” most nearly suggests that the leaves are
options: a piece of their shared place that Ivy can savor privately, without having to reply.
a reminder of the home Ronan hopes Ivy will one day come back to and settle in.
a costly gift meant to show Ivy how well the plantation has prospered since then.
a sign of the distance that has turned Ronan and Ivy into strangers to each other.
items.explanation: Ronan은 Ivy가 이제 달력을 지키지 않는다는 편지를 떠올리고 '그녀가 답해야 할 것은 아무것도' 보내지 않기로 한다. 함께 걷던 차밭의 잎을 보내며 그것을 '혼자 우려 마실 작은 나라'라고 부르므로, 두 단서를 이으면 공유한 장소의 한 조각을 부담 없이 홀로 즐기게 한다는 A가 정답이다. B는 귀환에 대한 바람을, C는 값비싼 과시를 가정하지만 지문에 근거가 없다. D는 거리를 말하지만 시는 단절이 아닌 배려를 그린다.

items.passage: Bailing with a soup pot, I stood knee-deep in the cellar of the Galway town hall in the spring of 1987 while Aoife, our mayor, held the torch. Somewhere down here, in a crate marked with a boy's surname, was his late grandfather's accordion, and Aoife had sworn to the boy at the funeral that it would be kept safe. She had said so before the river rose, before anyone knew the drains would fail. Even I, Chiara, the town's only doctor, have made my share of reckless reassurances at bedsides, so I did not scold her. Her promise, I thought, had been a paper boat set on a calm puddle, and now the puddle was a flood. We found the crate on a high shelf, damp at one corner, and Aoife laughed so hard she nearly dropped the torch. Upstairs, the clerk was ringing every household on the low road.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a paper boat set on a calm puddle” most nearly suggests that Aoife's promise was
options: a playful game that she never intended the boy to take seriously.
sincere but made before she could foresee the danger to come.
carefully planned to withstand any disaster the town might face.
a political gesture designed to win favor with the boy's family.
items.explanation: Aoife는 강물이 불어나기 전, 배수구가 막힐 줄 아무도 몰랐을 때 약속을 했고, 의사인 화자도 병상에서 무모한 안심의 말을 해 본 적이 있다며 그녀를 탓하지 않는다. 종이배는 진심으로 띄웠지만 연약한 것이고 '잔잔한 웅덩이'는 위험을 예견할 수 없던 상황을 뜻하므로 B가 정답이다. A는 '종이배'의 놀이 이미지만 취했고, C는 연약함과 정반대다. D의 정치적 의도는 지문에 단서가 없다.

items.passage: When we came back to Jeju Island in the autumn of 1898, my father, Taeyang, would not walk past the cemetery gate where his own father lay. He had left the island a young man and returned with a daughter who spoke English better than Korean, and I think he feared the dead would hear the difference. Each Sunday I, Gil, asked whether we might go in, and each Sunday he said the path was too muddy. Yet by midwinter he had begun stopping at the gate to straighten its leaning post, and once I saw him brush the moss from the nearest stone with his cuff. His refusal, I understood, had worn as thin as a winter sleeve. In March he asked me to teach him the English word for chrysanthemum, though he never said why. The gate creaked on its hinge as the wind came off the sea.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “worn as thin as a winter sleeve” most nearly suggests that Taeyang's
options: reasons for avoiding the cemetery had always been weak and insincere.
health had been steadily failing during the cold island winter.
resistance had gradually weakened until it barely held at all.
poverty had left him unable to afford proper graveside offerings.
items.explanation: 처음에 Taeyang은 매주 길이 질다며 묘지에 들어가기를 거부했지만, 한겨울쯤에는 문 기둥을 바로 세우고 소맷부리로 비석의 이끼를 닦는다. 오래 입어 닳은 겨울 소매처럼 그의 거부가 서서히 약해져 거의 남지 않았다는 뜻이므로 C가 정답이다. A는 '얇다'를 처음부터 약했다는 뜻으로 오독했고, 지문은 점진적 변화를 보여 준다. B는 겨울과 건강을, D는 낡은 옷과 가난을 문자적으로 연결한 오답이다.

items.passage: Years later, I still remember the cold of that monastery guesthouse outside Krakow, where Haruto and I had come to rest after our last season together on the stage. A rumor had followed us from the city: that I, Anushka, had complained to the director about her timing and asked to have her solo cut. It was half true, and it had been meant for no one's ears but the director's. When the porter repeated it to Haruto over breakfast, I braced for the sharp, icy silence she had once turned on a careless stagehand. Haruto, however, seemed entirely ______: she poured my tea, asked after my sore knee, and spoke of the rumor the way one might mention yesterday's weather. I left my tea untouched and went to watch the monks sweep the snow from the steps.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: vindictive
bewildered
remorseful
unruffled
items.explanation: 'however'는 화자가 예상한 날카롭고 차가운 침묵과 반대되는 반응을 예고하고, 이어지는 콜론 뒤에서 Haruto는 차를 따르고 무릎 안부를 묻고 소문을 어제 날씨 이야기하듯 말한다. 두 단서를 연결하면 동요하지 않고 침착했다는 뜻의 D 'unruffled'가 들어가야 한다. A 'vindictive'는 화자가 예상한 반응이라 however와 맞지 않는다. B 'bewildered'는 당황을, C 'remorseful'은 후회를 뜻하는데 소문의 당사자는 Haruto가 아니라 화자이므로 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Market noise forgives nothing. Baraka had told her new daughter-in-law this on the first morning, and now, between the stalls of smoked fish and indigo cloth in Accra, Obinna understood why. They were rehearsing the song Obinna would sing at the family's thanksgiving service on Sunday, and every time a vendor's call swallowed a high note, Baraka made her begin again. Some of the traders laughed at how many times the bride was stopped. Yet Baraka never raised her voice, and after each attempt she named the one phrase that had wavered and hummed it back, note by note, until Obinna could match it. Her coaching was ______, not cruel: she demanded nothing she had not first shown the girl how to reach. By noon, a woman selling plantains had begun to hum along under her breath.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: exacting
indifferent
hostile
lenient
items.explanation: Baraka는 높은 음이 묻힐 때마다 처음부터 다시 부르게 하지만 목소리를 높이지 않고, 흔들린 소절을 짚어 직접 불러 보이며 따라 하게 한다. 이 두 단서와 'not cruel'을 연결하면 엄격하고 까다롭지만 잔인하지는 않다는 A 'exacting'이 가장 정확하다. B 'indifferent'는 세심하게 지도하는 모습과 맞지 않고, C 'hostile'은 'not cruel'과 충돌한다. D 'lenient'는 계속 다시 시키는 태도와 반대다.

items.passage:
We who keep the lamps along the dock
have watched them meet here every evening for a week:
Linh with her novel in its blue cover,
Narong with the version he made of it,
his ending gentler than the one she wrote.
She has not shouted. She has not left.
Tonight she hands his pages back to him
and says the boat may sail with his words aboard,
but she keeps a pencil behind her ear
and asks to read each chapter before the printer does.
Her pardon is ______, a plank laid down
where the next one may still be lifted.
Out on the lake of Surabaya, a fisherman
shakes the water from his net and rows for home.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: absolute
provisional
insincere
hasty
items.explanation: Linh은 번역본을 돌려주며 출간을 허락하지만 연필을 귀에 꽂아 두고 인쇄 전에 모든 장을 읽겠다고 조건을 붙인다. 이어지는 '다음 판자는 아직 들어 올릴 수 있는 곳에 놓은 판자'라는 비유까지 연결하면, 그녀의 용서는 조건부라는 B 'provisional'이 들어가야 한다. A 'absolute'는 조건을 붙인 행동과 맞지 않는다. C 'insincere'는 그녀가 실제로 허락한다는 점과, D 'hasty'는 일주일 동안 매일 만나 고민했다는 점과 충돌한다.

items.passage: “Admiration doesn't fire the kiln,” Tommaso said, the first week I worked in his studio in Dhaka. I was nineteen and restless, convinced that the crowds who drifted in each Friday to photograph his glazes would soon become buyers. They praised everything: the speckled celadon, the bowls thin as eggshell, the way he trimmed a foot ring without looking. Yet month after month the shelves stayed full, and the electric bill went unpaid until Tommaso sold another wheel. I began to see why he greeted every compliment with a polite nod and returned at once to the wedging table. To him, praise that never became payment was ______, pleasant to hear but empty of anything he could use. Last spring I opened my own small studio, and I still keep a jar of his trimmings by the door.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: sincere
offensive
hollow
rare
items.explanation: Tommaso는 첫 주부터 '감탄은 가마에 불을 지펴 주지 않는다'고 말했고, 사람들이 모든 작품을 칭찬해도 선반은 그대로 차 있고 전기료조차 밀린다. 빈칸 뒤의 '듣기에는 좋지만 쓸 수 있는 것은 비어 있는'이라는 설명까지 연결하면 겉만 그럴듯하고 실속이 없다는 C 'hollow'가 정답이다. A 'sincere'는 칭찬의 진정성을 말할 뿐 '비어 있다'와 맞지 않고, B 'offensive'는 그가 공손히 고개를 끄덕인 태도와 충돌한다. D 'rare'는 매주 칭찬이 쏟아진다는 내용과 반대다.

items.passage: I was fifteen when Yoav, the foreman of the projection booth above the old hall in Haifa, hired me, Beulah, to rewind the reels after the last showing. On my first night he sketched a route home on the back of a handbill, and I laughed at it. His line looped up past the mosque, doubled back along the rope-makers' lane, and wound three streets out of my way before it reached my mother's door. I told him the path was absurdly ______, that I could be home in half the time by cutting across the lower wadi. He only tapped the handbill and said the lamps were lit on his streets. Two weeks later a carter was robbed in the dark of that wadi, and I folded his map into my coat pocket. Even now, the smell of warm film and machine oil brings back the narrow stair to that booth.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: direct
secretive
hazardous
circuitous
items.explanation: Yoav의 길은 모스크 위로 돌아가고 밧줄 장인 골목을 되짚으며 세 블록이나 우회하고, 화자는 지름길로 가면 절반 시간이면 된다고 반박한다. 두 단서를 연결하면 화자가 비웃은 것은 길이 터무니없이 돌아간다는 점이므로 D 'circuitous'가 정답이다. A 'direct'는 우회와 정반대다. C 'hazardous'는 위험했던 것이 오히려 지름길인 와디였으므로 맞지 않고, B 'secretive'는 길의 특성과 관련된 단서가 없다.

items.passage: Wringing out a cloth in the basin, Savitri listened to the pickers singing below the veranda of the vineyard house outside Mumbai. Her patient, Sharda, had not slept for three nights, and tonight she was in a mood to accuse. Had Savitri not insisted on the fever cure, Sharda declared, she would have been fit to travel to the conservatory in Poona and sing for its masters; the letter had come and gone while she lay here. Savitri set her jaw and recited, in a clipped voice, every dose of physic she had measured out. Then Sharda's hand slid across the coverlet and closed on her wrist, and the old woman whispered that she had known for years her voice was gone, that it was easier to blame a nurse than a throat. Savitri sat down slowly on the edge of the bed. She told Sharda about the grape baskets stacked by the press, purple to the brim, and Sharda listened with her eyes closed, smiling. Down the hill, the singing stopped, and a lantern moved toward the sheds.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: It moves from defensive tension to gentle sympathy once Sharda confesses why she blamed Savitri.
It moves from cheerful hope to bitter resentment after Sharda learns the conservatory rejected her.
It moves from calm routine to sudden alarm as Sharda's fever grows worse during the long night.
It moves from quiet sorrow to playful teasing as Savitri describes the grape harvest to Sharda.
items.explanation: 처음에 Sharda는 기회를 놓친 책임을 Savitri에게 돌리고, Savitri는 턱을 굳힌 채 딱딱한 목소리로 투약 기록을 읊어 방어적 긴장이 흐른다. 그러다 Sharda가 목소리는 이미 오래전에 사라졌고 목보다 간호사를 탓하는 게 쉬웠다고 고백하자, Savitri는 천천히 침대에 앉아 포도 이야기를 들려준다. 따라서 긴장에서 다정한 공감으로 바뀐다는 A가 정답이다. B는 거절 통보가 없고, C는 열이 악화되지 않으며, D는 장난스러운 분위기로 볼 근거가 없다.

items.passage: When Brigid swept into the dining hall of the boys' summer camp outside Glasgow, she meant to have it out with Esteban before the soup was served. Her brother had written home of a broken window and a week of extra lessons, and the tutor, it seemed, had told the camp master nothing at all about who had thrown the stone. Brigid laid the letter beside his plate and demanded to know what sort of guardian kept such things from a family. Esteban folded his napkin with great care. The stone, he said quietly, had been thrown at her brother, not by him, and the boys who threw it were the sons of the men who paid for the camp. Had he spoken, it was her brother who would have been sent home. Brigid sat down on the bench across from him, and for some time neither of them touched the bread. At the far end of the hall, a bell was rung for grace, and two hundred chairs scraped at once.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: from playful teasing to open hostility as Brigid learns about the broken window
from indignant accusation to sober understanding as Esteban explains his silence
from anxious worry to cheerful relief as Brigid learns her brother is unharmed
from formal politeness to bitter despair as Esteban admits he has failed the boy
items.explanation: Brigid는 식당에 뛰어들어 편지를 내밀며 어떤 보호자가 가족에게 그런 일을 숨기느냐고 따져 분개한 어조로 시작한다. Esteban이 돌은 동생을 향해 던져졌고 말했다면 오히려 동생이 쫓겨났을 것이라고 설명하자, 그녀는 맞은편에 앉아 한동안 빵에 손대지 않는다. 따라서 분노한 추궁에서 숙연한 이해로 바뀐다는 B가 정답이다. A는 장난스러운 시작이, C는 밝은 안도가, D는 Esteban의 실패 인정이 지문에 없다.

items.passage: Years later, the daughter would write that she had never hated anyone so thoroughly as the crowd at the Bologna ferry terminal on the morning her mother fainted against the ticket rail. Her mother had insisted on traveling alone, had refused the daughter's arm on the stairs, and then had crumpled in front of forty strangers, her hat rolling under a bench. The daughter remembered every stare and every whisper, and she recorded them in her diary with a cold, exact fury. But the essay turns on the next detail: Giacomo, the porter, retrieving the hat, brushing it with his sleeve, and handing it not to the daughter but to the mother, as though she were a lady who had merely dropped it. From that point the daughter's sentences loosen. She describes her mother pinning the hat back on with trembling dignity, and the two of them laughing, later, over the porter's grand bow. The ferry, she notes, left forty minutes late that day, its whistle echoing along the canal.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: from cheerful nostalgia to sudden grief when the mother collapses at the terminal
from calm reporting to anxious urgency as the daughter rushes to find medical help
from bitter resentment to warm gratitude after Giacomo's courteous gesture
from amused mockery to quiet shame as the daughter recalls her own rudeness
items.explanation: 처음에 딸은 군중을 그토록 미워한 적이 없다고 쓰고, 모든 시선과 속삭임을 차갑고 정확한 분노로 일기에 적는다. 그런데 짐꾼 Giacomo가 모자를 주워 어머니에게 숙녀를 대하듯 건넨 뒤로 문장이 풀리고, 어머니의 떨리는 위엄과 나중의 웃음이 그려진다. 따라서 쓰라린 원망에서 따뜻한 고마움으로 바뀐다는 C가 정답이다. A는 시작이 밝지 않고, B는 의료 도움을 구하는 장면이 없으며, D는 딸이 무례했다는 단서가 없다.

items.passage: “You always did eat too fast,” Leopoldina said, as Thiago bent over his bowl at the noodle stall behind the cemetery in Lisbon. It was the spring of 1924, and they had not spoken in eleven years. The funeral of their grandmother had brought them back to the same table, and the question of what to do with Leopoldina's aging father hung between them like steam. Thiago thought the old man should come to Porto; Leopoldina said he would wither away from the river. They argued in short, cool sentences, each correcting the other's memory of whose fault the long silence had been. Then the stall keeper set down a dish of fried dough without being asked, and Thiago recognized it as the treat their grandmother had bought them every Sunday as children. Leopoldina laughed despite herself and pushed the plate toward him. They began to talk of her father's fig tree, and of how he might be persuaded to visit both cities in turn. A tram rattled past, scattering pigeons from the cobbles.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: from mournful grief to playful mockery as the cousins begin teasing the stall keeper
from warm nostalgia to bitter dispute over who will inherit their grandmother's house
from polite formality to open anger when Thiago insists on moving the father to Porto
from guarded argument to renewed warmth after a reminder of their shared childhood
items.explanation: 사촌들은 처음에 아버지를 어디로 모실지를 두고 짧고 차가운 문장으로 다투며 오랜 침묵이 누구 탓인지 서로 바로잡는다. 노점 주인이 할머니가 어린 시절 매주 사 주던 튀김 과자를 내오자 Leopoldina가 웃으며 접시를 밀어 주고, 둘은 무화과나무와 두 도시를 오가는 방안을 이야기한다. 따라서 경계 어린 논쟁에서 공유한 추억을 계기로 따뜻함을 되찾는다는 D가 정답이다. A의 조롱, B의 유산 다툼, C의 공공연한 분노는 지문의 흐름과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: We had rented the school gymnasium in Kingston for the reception because it was cheap and because my mother had taught there for thirty years. That Saturday we walked its floor with a tape measure, arguing over where the long tables should go and whether Dwayne's band needed a riser. In the corner sat the one thing left from her house on Hope Road, which we had finished emptying that morning: a battered upright piano. My mother lifted its lid and played the first bars of the hymn she had used to end every school assembly, and I, Roshane, remembered sitting cross-legged on this very floor, listening to her. When she closed the lid, we did not return to the tables at once. Instead we measured again, this time to find a space beside the stage where the piano could stand on the day itself. Outside, a groundskeeper was chalking white lines across the football pitch.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It moves from routine planning to a memory sparked by an object, then back to reshaped planning.
It describes a long quarrel between mother and daughter and then explains how they resolved it.
It lists the items removed from a house and then judges which were most valuable to the family.
It presents the daughter's doubts about the wedding and then shows her mother easing them.
items.explanation: 글은 체육관에서 줄자로 테이블 위치와 무대를 두고 실무적으로 계획하는 장면으로 시작한다. 이어 집에서 남은 마지막 물건인 피아노를 어머니가 연주하자 화자가 어린 시절 같은 바닥에 앉아 듣던 기억을 떠올리고, 이후 피아노를 놓을 자리를 찾기 위해 다시 측정하며 계획의 목적이 바뀐다. 따라서 계획→물건이 불러온 기억→바뀐 계획의 구조인 A가 정답이다. B의 오랜 다툼, C의 물건 목록 평가, D의 결혼에 대한 의심은 지문에 없다.
